spatial_claims.claim: Points A, C, B, D are collinear in that order with AC = CB (AB bisected at C, BD added beyond B)
E is placed on the extension of BA beyond A with AE = BD; point order becomes E, A, C, B, D on a single line
EC = EA + AC (A is between E and C, so segments add); CD = CB + BD (B is between C and D, so segments add)
EC = CD, so C is the midpoint of ED
A cuts ED into unequal segments EA and AD, with AD > EA
ED is bisected at C and cut unequally at A; the segment between the points of section is CA = AC; 2.9 applies to give S(EA) + S(AD) = 2S(EC) + 2S(AC)
spatial_claims.type: application of prior identity to collinear configuration

spatial_claims.claim: EA = BD and EC = CD are substituted into the identity from Step 4

configuration_map: All points lie on a single straight line in the order E, A, C, B, D. Key relationships: AC = CB (given, bisection of AB), AE = BD (constructed), EC = EA + AC = BD + CB = CD (derived, so C bisects ED). Point A lies between E and C, dividing ED into unequal segments EA (shorter) and AD (longer). The entire proof operates on this one-dimensional collinear configuration with no auxiliary points off the line, no angles, no triangles, and no circles. Proposition 2.9 is applied to line ED with bisection point C and unequal cut point A.
pass_reason: All spatial claims involve collinear points on a single line in the order E, A, C, B, D. The betweenness relations, segment additions, and bisection claims are all mutually consistent. The application of 2.9 to line ED (bisected at C, cut unequally at A) is valid since both C and A lie on ED with the required properties. There are no angle decompositions, no inside/outside claims, and no complex geometric configurations that could harbor contradictions. The proof is a sound algebraic manipulation of segment relationships on a line.
